records.question: does vitamin d reduce mortality
records.answer: Overall, vitamin D supplementation decreased mortality in randomized trials (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.00) [4]. Only vitamin D3 significantly decreased mortality (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.91 to 0.98), whereas vitamin D2, alfacalcidol, and calcitriol did not [4].

records.question: is red meat linked to colorectal cancer
records.answer:
Yes — prospective meta-analyses found that red and processed meat intake was associated with increased colorectal cancer risk (summary RR 1.22 for highest vs lowest intake; RR 1.14 per 100 g/day) [1].  
Other reviews report a modest 20–30% increased risk for high consumers of cured and red meat, and case-control studies have linked meat-related compounds (HCAs, PAHs, nitrites/nitrates) to colorectal cancer and subsite-specific tumors [3][4].

records.question: what are the effects of dietary fiber on cholesterol
records.answer: A very-high-fiber vegetable, fruit, and nut diet produced the largest reduction in LDL cholesterol (33% ± 4%) compared with starch-based and low-fat diets in a 2-week controlled study of ten healthy volunteers [1]. Regular consumption of dietary fiber, particularly cereal fiber, may improve cardiovascular health through multiple mechanisms including lipid reduction [3].

records.question: does green tea help with weight loss
records.answer:
Laboratory studies have demonstrated the potential efficacy of green or black tea for the prevention of obesity [1].  
Results of human intervention studies are mixed and the role of caffeine in any effect has not been clearly established [1].

what is the effect of soy on breast cancer risk
records.answer:
In high-soy-consuming Asian studies, increasing soy food intake was associated with decreased breast cancer risk, with OR=0.88 (≈10 mg isoflavones/day) and OR=0.71 (≥20 mg/day) compared to ≤5 mg/day [1].  
In contrast, studies in low-soy-consuming Western populations found soy intake was unrelated to breast cancer risk [1].  
Other studies report that high soy intake during adolescence or consistent high intake is associated with reduced premenopausal breast cancer risk and that associations may vary by ER/PR status [5][4].

records.question: does coffee consumption affect liver disease
records.answer: Observational studies and meta-analyses report that coffee consumption is associated with a reduced risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and liver cancer, with summary relative risks/odds ratios around 0.44–0.80 for higher versus no consumption and a reported 40% reduced HCC risk for any coffee consumption versus none in one meta-analysis [1][4]. Coffee intake has also been associated with lower mortality from chronic liver disease in cohort studies and with lower liver enzymes and reduced oxidative/collagen markers during coffee consumption in a randomized trial [5][2].

records.question: is there a link between dairy and prostate cancer
records.answer: Yes — several epidemiological studies and reviews report that higher milk or dairy consumption is associated with an increased risk of prostate cancer [1][5][3]. Mechanistic reviews propose roles for milk-derived hormones, IGF-1, and milk-stimulated mTORC1 signaling in promoting prostate cancer development or progression [2][4].

records.question: what are the cardiovascular effects of omega 3
records.answer:
Omega-3 fatty acids have an antiarrhythmic effect that may be particularly crucial for men at high risk of sudden death [1].  
Intake of alpha-linolenic acid (an omega-3) from walnuts and flax was associated with reductions in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and several markers of inflammation [4].  
Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids were associated with decreased serum triglycerides and demonstrated hypotriglyceridemic and anti-inflammatory effects, with decreases in insulin resistance and inflammatory markers seen in one survey [5].
